igcse-0580-rates-pay-exchange.description: Read a rate as an amount per one unit, then choose whether to multiply or divide.

sections.title: What does ‘per hour’ mean?
sections.label: Rates per one unit
sections.intro: A rate compares two different quantities. ‘Per hour’ tells you the amount for one hour.

blocks.html: Multiply the hourly rate by hours when you know the time. Divide total pay by hours to find the rate for one hour.

figure.alt: A time strip shows two full hours and one half-hour at the same hourly rate.
figure.caption: The half-hour contributes half of the amount earned in any full hour.

blocks.title: Apply an hourly rate
blocks.prompt: A gallery guide earns £12.32 an hour. What are the wages for 2 hours 30 minutes?
blocks.hint: Change the minutes to a fraction of an hour before multiplying.
blocks.solution:
30 minutes is \(0.5\,\mathrm h\), so the shift lasts \(2.5\,\mathrm h\).

Each hour earns £12.32. Multiply by the number of hours using \(12.32\times 2.5=30.8\).

The wages are £30.80.

blocks.html: A shift of 2 hours 30 minutes is \(2.5\) hours. The 30 minutes must be expressed as part of 60 minutes.

blocks.title: Find a wage per hour
blocks.prompt: A workshop assistant earns £36.00 for \(3\,\mathrm h\) of work at one rate. Find the hourly rate in pounds.
blocks.hint: The number of hours is the denominator when you calculate pay per hour.
blocks.solution:
The pay is spread evenly over \(3\) hours.

Find the pay for one hour with \(\frac{36}{3}=12\).

The rate is £12.00 per hour.

blocks.html: Check the order of the units in a rate before choosing which number to divide by.

sections.title: How do I recover a missing time or combine pay?
sections.label: Missing time and separate periods
sections.intro: Ask which quantity you know. When you know the total and the rate for one hour, find how many one-hour amounts fit into the total.

blocks.html: Divide wages by pay per hour to recover hours. With more than one rate, calculate the pay for each period before adding the totals.

blocks.title: Recover time from total wages
blocks.prompt: A kiosk pays £15.00 per hour and paid £37.50 for one shift. How many hours did the shift last?
blocks.hint: Divide by the amount earned in one hour.
blocks.solution:
Each hour accounts for one copy of the hourly wage.

Divide the full pay by the pay for one hour. \(\frac{37.5}{15}=2.5\).

The shift lasted \(2.5\,\mathrm h\).

blocks.html: Two stated pay rates may apply for different lengths of time. They cannot be added to form one hourly rate.

blocks.title: Apply two pay rates to separate blocks
blocks.prompt: A caretaker works 2 hours at £13.00 per hour, then \(2\) hours at £18.00 per hour. Find the total pay.
blocks.hint: Use each rate for its own time. Add the pay amounts after calculating them separately.
blocks.solution:
The first block earns £26.00 from the first rate and time.

The second block earns £36.00 from the second rate and time.

Together these earnings are £62.00.

blocks.html: Write the unit for each intermediate value. Pounds divided by pounds per hour give hours.

sections.title: Which way do I use an exchange rate?
sections.label: Exchange direction
sections.intro: Identify the currency you start with and the one you want. Start with the pair of amounts written in the exchange rate.

blocks.html: If £1 is worth €1.16, multiply a pound amount by 1.16 to get euros. Divide a euro amount by 1.16 to go back to pounds.

blocks.title: Convert from the one-unit currency
blocks.prompt: For a classroom example, £1.00 exchanges for €1.15. At this rate, how many euros is £41.00?
blocks.hint: The rate gives euros for one pound. Start with pounds and scale both sides by the same factor.
blocks.solution:
The given rate is €1.15 for every pound.

Multiply the number of pounds by the euros per pound. \(41\times 1.15=47.15\).

The exchanged amount is €47.15.

blocks.html: The number 1.16 represents euros per pound. Using it to multiply in both directions changes the amount incorrectly.

blocks.title: Convert back at the stated rate
blocks.prompt: The exchange rate in this question is £1.00 to €1.20. Work out the number of pounds that corresponds to €34.80.
blocks.hint: The amount you start with is in euros. Divide by the number of euros for one pound.
blocks.solution:
Every €1.20 represents one pound.

Find the number of groups of €1.20 in the euro amount. \(\frac{34.8}{1.2}=29\).

The amount in pounds is £29.00.

blocks.html: Make a short line with £1 and its equivalent in euros before working with the amount you are given.

examples.title: Apply an hourly rate
examples.question: A gallery guide earns £12.00 an hour. What are the wages for 2 hours 15 minutes?
solution: 15 minutes is \(0.25\,\mathrm h\), so the shift lasts \(2.25\,\mathrm h\).
Each hour earns £12.00. Multiply by the number of hours using \(12\times 2.25=27\).
The wages are £27.00.

examples.title: Find a wage per hour
examples.question: A workshop assistant earns £28.75 for \(2.5\,\mathrm h\) of work at one rate. Find the hourly rate in pounds.
solution: The pay is spread evenly over \(2.5\) hours.
Find the pay for one hour with \(\frac{28.75}{2.5}=11.5\).
The rate is £11.50 per hour.

examples.title: Recover time from total wages
examples.question: A kiosk pays £14.00 per hour and paid £31.50 for one shift. How many hours did the shift last?
solution: Each hour accounts for one copy of the hourly wage.
Divide the full pay by the pay for one hour. \(\frac{31.5}{14}=2.25\).
The shift lasted \(2.25\,\mathrm h\).

examples.title: Apply two pay rates to separate blocks
examples.question: A caretaker works 1 hours at £12.00 per hour, then \(1.5\) hours at £16.00 per hour. Find the total pay.
solution: The first block earns £12.00 from the first rate and time.
The second block earns £24.00 from the second rate and time.
Together these earnings are £36.00.

examples.title: Convert from the one-unit currency
examples.question: For a classroom example, £1.00 exchanges for €1.13. At this rate, how many euros is £37.00?
solution: The given rate is €1.13 for every pound.
Multiply the number of pounds by the euros per pound. \(37\times 1.13=41.81\).
The exchanged amount is €41.81.

examples.title: Convert back at the stated rate
examples.question: The exchange rate in this question is £1.00 to €1.19. Work out the number of pounds that corresponds to €28.56.
solution: Every €1.19 represents one pound.
Find the number of groups of €1.19 in the euro amount. \(\frac{28.56}{1.19}=24\).
The amount in pounds is £24.00.

extraPractice.title: Apply an hourly rate
extraPractice.prompt: A gallery guide earns £12.64 an hour. What are the wages for 2 hours 45 minutes?
extraPractice.hint: Change the minutes to a fraction of an hour before multiplying.
extraPractice.solution:
45 minutes is \(0.75\,\mathrm h\), so the shift lasts \(2.75\,\mathrm h\).

extraPractice.title: Find a wage per hour

extraPractice.hint: The number of hours is the denominator when you calculate pay per hour.
extraPractice.solution:
The pay is spread evenly over \(3.5\) hours.

Find the pay for one hour with \(\frac{43.75}{3.5}=12.5\).

extraPractice.title: Recover time from total wages

extraPractice.hint: Divide by the amount earned in one hour.
extraPractice.solution:

extraPractice.title: Apply two pay rates to separate blocks
extraPractice.prompt: A caretaker works 3 hours at £14.00 per hour, then \(2.5\) hours at £20.00 per hour. Find the total pay.
extraPractice.hint: Use each rate for its own time. Add the pay amounts after calculating them separately.
extraPractice.solution:
The first block earns £42.00 from the first rate and time.

The second block earns £50.00 from the second rate and time.

Together these earnings are £92.00.

extraPractice.title: Convert from the one-unit currency
extraPractice.prompt: For a classroom example, £1.00 exchanges for €1.17. At this rate, how many euros is £45.00?
extraPractice.hint: The rate gives euros for one pound. Start with pounds and scale both sides by the same factor.
extraPractice.solution:
The given rate is €1.17 for every pound.

Multiply the number of pounds by the euros per pound. \(45\times 1.17=52.65\).

The exchanged amount is €52.65.

extraPractice.title: Convert back at the stated rate
extraPractice.prompt: The exchange rate in this question is £1.00 to €1.21. Work out the number of pounds that corresponds to €41.14.
extraPractice.hint: The amount you start with is in euros. Divide by the number of euros for one pound.
extraPractice.solution:
Every €1.21 represents one pound.

Find the number of groups of €1.21 in the euro amount. \(\frac{41.14}{1.21}=34\).

The amount in pounds is £34.00.

glossary.definition: An amount of one quantity for a stated amount of another.
The pay earned for one hour at a stated rate.
The amount of one currency given for a stated amount of another.
For each or for one.
A period of time at work.

revision.body:
Rates per one unit

Multiply the hourly rate by hours when you know the time. Divide total pay by hours to find the rate for one hour.

Missing time and separate periods

Divide wages by pay per hour to recover hours. With more than one rate, calculate the pay for each period before adding the totals.

Exchange direction

If £1 is worth €1.16, multiply a pound amount by 1.16 to get euros. Divide a euro amount by 1.16 to go back to pounds.

Example

A shift lasts \(2.5\) hours at £12 per hour. The total pay is \(12\times2.5=30\) pounds.

Check yourself

  • At £14 per hour, how much is earned in 45 minutes?
  • At a rate of £1 to €1.16, find the value of €58 in pounds.

Answers £10.50 and £50.00.
revision.checks:
• A shift of 2 hours 30 minutes is \(2.5\) hours. The 30 minutes must be expressed as part of 60 minutes.
  • Two stated pay rates may apply for different lengths of time. They cannot be added to form one hourly rate.
  • The number 1.16 represents euros per pound. Using it to multiply in both directions changes the amount incorrectly.
revision.examTip: Make a short line with £1 and its equivalent in euros before working with the amount you are given.

igcse-0580-rates-flow-fuel.description: Connect volume with time and litres of fuel with a stated distance.

sections.title: How do I find the rate or filling time?
sections.label: Volume and time
sections.intro: A flow rate describes volume passing in a given time. A rate in litres per minute tells you how much arrives in one minute.

blocks.html: Divide the delivered volume by minutes to find litres per minute. Multiply rate by minutes to find the delivered volume.

figure.alt: A gauge shows a starting volume of 5 litres and a target of 13 litres.
figure.caption: Fill from 5 L to 13 L. Only the difference is supplied by the pump.

blocks.title: Find volume per minute
blocks.prompt: A refill pump delivers \(12\,\mathrm L\) in 4 minutes. Find its average flow rate in litres per minute.
blocks.hint: Divide the volume by the time in minutes.
blocks.solution:
The numerator is volume in litres. The denominator is time in minutes.

Find litres for one minute with \(\frac{12}{4}=3\).

The average rate is \(3\,\mathrm{L/min}\).

blocks.html: If there is already liquid in the tank, find the increase needed. The pump does not supply the starting volume again.

blocks.title: Fill only the missing volume
blocks.prompt: A tank already contains \(6\,\mathrm L\). A pump adds \(4\,\mathrm{L/min}\). How many minutes are needed to reach \(30\,\mathrm L\)?
blocks.hint: The pump only supplies the increase, not all the water in the tank.
blocks.solution:
Subtract the starting volume from the target. The pump must add \(24\,\mathrm L\).

Divide the volume to add by the supply in one minute. \(\frac{24}{4}=6\).

The time needed is \(6\,\mathrm{min}\).

blocks.html: Show the new volume added separately from the starting and target readings.

sections.title: How do I change the reference amount?
sections.label: Convert the units and scale
sections.intro: For a flow rate, you can change the volume unit and the reference time. For fuel consumption, scale the reference distance to the length of the trip.

blocks.html: There are 60 seconds in a minute and 1000 millilitres in a litre. A flow of \(50\,\mathrm{mL/s}\) delivers 3000 mL in one minute, which is \(3\,\mathrm{L/min}\).

blocks.title: Change millilitres per second to litres per minute
blocks.prompt: A dosing pipe supplies \(40\,\mathrm{mL/s}\). Give the same flow in litres per minute.
blocks.hint: Convert the time interval first. Then convert the volume to litres.
blocks.solution:
Sixty seconds make one minute. A minute delivers \(2400\,\mathrm{mL}\).

Since 1000 mL make 1 L, divide the volume in millilitres by 1000.

The flow is \(2.4\,\mathrm{L/min}\).

blocks.html: Changing seconds to minutes changes the number of intervals covered. Convert the time and volume as separate steps.

blocks.title: Use litres per hundred kilometres
blocks.prompt: A van uses \(6.6\,\mathrm L\) of fuel for each \(100\,\mathrm{km}\). How many litres are used over \(150\,\mathrm{km}\) at the same consumption rate?
blocks.hint: First work out how many groups of 100 km the journey represents.
blocks.solution:
The trip is \(1.5\) times 100 km.

Use the same multiplier on the litres. \(6.6\times 1.5=9.9\).

The van uses \(9.9\,\mathrm L\).

blocks.html: State whether an intermediate number represents volume, time or a rate.

sections.title: How do I use litres per 100 kilometres?
sections.label: Read the reference distance
sections.intro: A fuel figure in litres per 100 km describes fuel used for a reference distance. A longer trip uses a proportional amount at the same rate.

blocks.html: Divide the trip distance by 100 to find how many reference distances it contains. Multiply that number by the stated litres. To find the rate from a trip, find litres per kilometre and multiply by 100.

blocks.title: Calculate fuel consumption per 100 km
blocks.prompt: A survey vehicle used \(14\,\mathrm L\) over \(250\,\mathrm{km}\). Find the fuel used per 100 km.
blocks.hint: The question asks for fuel per 100 km, not kilometres per litre.
blocks.solution:
Divide \(14\,\mathrm L\) by \(250\,\mathrm{km}\) to find litres per kilometre.

Multiply that rate by 100 to cover one hundred kilometres. \(\frac{14}{250}\times100=5.6\).

The consumption is \(5.6\,\mathrm L\) per 100 km.

blocks.html: Litres per 100 km and kilometres per litre describe the same idea with the quantities in different positions. Read the requested unit.

blocks.title: Find distance from available fuel
blocks.prompt: A field vehicle on a survey route uses \(7\,\mathrm L\) for every 100 km. At the same rate, how far could it travel using \(17.5\,\mathrm L\)?
blocks.hint: Work out how many 100 km portions the available litres can supply.
blocks.solution:
Each \(7\,\mathrm L\) supplies one 100 km interval.

The fuel allows \(2.5\) intervals, found by dividing the litres by \(7\).

Multiply by 100 km. The distance is \(250\,\mathrm{km}\).

blocks.html: Show which distance the litres belong to. Keep the 100 km reference in the written answer.

examples.title: Find volume per minute
examples.question: A refill pump delivers \(8.4\,\mathrm L\) in 3 minutes. Find its average flow rate in litres per minute.
solution: The numerator is volume in litres. The denominator is time in minutes.
Find litres for one minute with \(\frac{8.4}{3}=2.8\).
The average rate is \(2.8\,\mathrm{L/min}\).

examples.title: Fill only the missing volume
examples.question: A tank already contains \(5\,\mathrm L\). A pump adds \(3.5\,\mathrm{L/min}\). How many minutes are needed to reach \(19\,\mathrm L\)?
solution: Subtract the starting volume from the target. The pump must add \(14\,\mathrm L\).
Divide the volume to add by the supply in one minute. \(\frac{14}{3.5}=4\).
The time needed is \(4\,\mathrm{min}\).

examples.title: Change millilitres per second to litres per minute
examples.question: A dosing pipe supplies \(35\,\mathrm{mL/s}\). Give the same flow in litres per minute.
solution: Sixty seconds make one minute. A minute delivers \(2100\,\mathrm{mL}\).
Since 1000 mL make 1 L, divide the volume in millilitres by 1000.
The flow is \(2.1\,\mathrm{L/min}\).

examples.title: Use litres per hundred kilometres
examples.question: A van uses \(6.2\,\mathrm L\) of fuel for each \(100\,\mathrm{km}\). How many litres are used over \(125\,\mathrm{km}\) at the same consumption rate?
solution: The trip is \(1.25\) times 100 km.
Use the same multiplier on the litres. \(6.2\times 1.25=7.75\).
The van uses \(7.75\,\mathrm L\).

examples.title: Calculate fuel consumption per 100 km
examples.question: A survey vehicle used \(10.8\,\mathrm L\) over \(200\,\mathrm{km}\). Find the fuel used per 100 km.
solution: Divide \(10.8\,\mathrm L\) by \(200\,\mathrm{km}\) to find litres per kilometre.
Multiply that rate by 100 to cover one hundred kilometres. \(\frac{10.8}{200}\times100=5.4\).
The consumption is \(5.4\,\mathrm L\) per 100 km.

examples.title: Find distance from available fuel
examples.question: A field vehicle on a survey route uses \(6.8\,\mathrm L\) for every 100 km. At the same rate, how far could it travel using \(15.3\,\mathrm L\)?
solution: Each \(6.8\,\mathrm L\) supplies one 100 km interval.
The fuel allows \(2.25\) intervals, found by dividing the litres by \(6.8\).
Multiply by 100 km. The distance is \(225\,\mathrm{km}\).

extraPractice.title: Find volume per minute
extraPractice.prompt: A refill pump delivers \(16\,\mathrm L\) in 5 minutes. Find its average flow rate in litres per minute.
extraPractice.hint: Divide the volume by the time in minutes.
extraPractice.solution:
The numerator is volume in litres. The denominator is time in minutes.

Find litres for one minute with \(\frac{16}{5}=3.2\).

The average rate is \(3.2\,\mathrm{L/min}\).

extraPractice.title: Fill only the missing volume
extraPractice.prompt: A tank already contains \(7\,\mathrm L\). A pump adds \(4.5\,\mathrm{L/min}\). How many minutes are needed to reach \(43\,\mathrm L\)?
extraPractice.hint: The pump only supplies the increase, not all the water in the tank.
extraPractice.solution:
Subtract the starting volume from the target. The pump must add \(36\,\mathrm L\).

Divide the volume to add by the supply in one minute. \(\frac{36}{4.5}=8\).

The time needed is \(8\,\mathrm{min}\).

extraPractice.title: Change millilitres per second to litres per minute
extraPractice.prompt: A dosing pipe supplies \(45\,\mathrm{mL/s}\). Give the same flow in litres per minute.
extraPractice.hint: Convert the time interval first. Then convert the volume to litres.
extraPractice.solution:
Sixty seconds make one minute. A minute delivers \(2700\,\mathrm{mL}\).

Since 1000 mL make 1 L, divide the volume in millilitres by 1000.

The flow is \(2.7\,\mathrm{L/min}\).

extraPractice.title: Use litres per hundred kilometres
extraPractice.prompt: A van uses \(7\,\mathrm L\) of fuel for each \(100\,\mathrm{km}\). How many litres are used over \(175\,\mathrm{km}\) at the same consumption rate?
extraPractice.hint: First work out how many groups of 100 km the journey represents.
extraPractice.solution:
The trip is \(1.75\) times 100 km.

Use the same multiplier on the litres. \(7\times 1.75=12.25\).

The van uses \(12.25\,\mathrm L\).

extraPractice.title: Calculate fuel consumption per 100 km
extraPractice.prompt: A survey vehicle used \(17.4\,\mathrm L\) over \(300\,\mathrm{km}\). Find the fuel used per 100 km.
extraPractice.hint: The question asks for fuel per 100 km, not kilometres per litre.
extraPractice.solution:
Divide \(17.4\,\mathrm L\) by \(300\,\mathrm{km}\) to find litres per kilometre.

Multiply that rate by 100 to cover one hundred kilometres. \(\frac{17.4}{300}\times100=5.8\).

The consumption is \(5.8\,\mathrm L\) per 100 km.

extraPractice.title: Find distance from available fuel
extraPractice.prompt: A field vehicle on a survey route uses \(7.2\,\mathrm L\) for every 100 km. At the same rate, how far could it travel using \(19.8\,\mathrm L\)?
extraPractice.hint: Work out how many 100 km portions the available litres can supply.
extraPractice.solution:
Each \(7.2\,\mathrm L\) supplies one 100 km interval.

The fuel allows \(2.75\) intervals, found by dividing the litres by \(7.2\).

Multiply by 100 km. The distance is \(275\,\mathrm{km}\).

glossary.definition: Volume supplied or passing per unit of time.
The distance named in a rate, such as 100 km.
The amount of fuel used for a specified distance.
The amount of space occupied.
A rate that stays the same during the calculation.

revision.body:
Volume and time

Divide the delivered volume by minutes to find litres per minute. Multiply rate by minutes to find the delivered volume.

Convert the units and scale

There are 60 seconds in a minute and 1000 millilitres in a litre. A flow of \(50\,\mathrm{mL/s}\) delivers 3000 mL in one minute, which is \(3\,\mathrm{L/min}\).

Read the reference distance

Divide the trip distance by 100 to find how many reference distances it contains. Multiply that number by the stated litres. To find the rate from a trip, find litres per kilometre and multiply by 100.

Example

A tank needs 8 more litres. At \(2\,\mathrm{L/min}\), it takes four minutes to supply the increase.

Check yourself

  • Change 45 mL/s to L/min.
  • A van uses 7 L per 100 km. How many litres does it use over 250 km?

Answers \(2.7\,\mathrm{L/min}\) and \(17.5\,\mathrm L\).
revision.checks:
• If there is already liquid in the tank, find the increase needed. The pump does not supply the starting volume again.
  • Changing seconds to minutes changes the number of intervals covered. Convert the time and volume as separate steps.
  • Litres per 100 km and kilometres per litre describe the same idea with the quantities in different positions. Read the requested unit.
revision.examTip: Show which distance the litres belong to. Keep the 100 km reference in the written answer.

igcse-0580-rates-compound-measures.description: Use a supplied compound-measure formula and check what each unit represents.

sections.title: What does a density value measure?
sections.label: Mass and volume
sections.intro: Density measures the mass for one unit of volume. Read the mass unit and the volume unit before substituting.

blocks.html: Use the supplied formula \(\text{density}=\frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}\). With grams and cubic centimetres, report grams per cubic centimetre.

blocks.title: Find mass per cubic centimetre
blocks.prompt: Use \(\text{density}=\frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}\). A sample has mass \(62.5\,\mathrm g\) and volume \(25\,\mathrm{cm}^3\). Find its density in grams per cubic centimetre.
blocks.hint: Density is the mass of one cubic centimetre under this model.
blocks.solution:
Substitute the mass as the numerator and the volume as the denominator.

\(\frac{62.5}{25}=2.5\).

The density is \(2.5\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}\).

field.label: Density in grams per cubic centimetre

blocks.html: If a question asks for mass, use the known density and volume to recover it. The value of density is not the total mass.

blocks.title: Recover mass from density and volume
blocks.prompt: Use \(\text{density}=\frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}\). A casting has volume \(40\,\mathrm{cm}^3\) and density \(1.4\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}\). Find its mass.
blocks.hint: Multiply the mass of one cubic centimetre by the number of cubic centimetres.
blocks.solution:
Multiply both sides of the given formula by volume to get mass.

Multiply grams per cubic centimetre by the volume. \(1.4\times 40=56\).

The mass is \(56\,\mathrm g\).

blocks.html: Check that the units in the quotient match the units requested.

sections.title: Which area belongs in the pressure formula?
sections.label: Force on a contact area
sections.intro: Pressure describes force per unit area. Use the part of the surface that the force acts on.

blocks.html: Use \(\text{pressure}=\frac{\text{force}}{\text{contact area}}\). With force in newtons and area in square metres, the unit is newtons per square metre. One square metre contains 10 000 square centimetres.

figure.alt: A downward force acts on a rectangular contact area.
figure.caption: Pressure uses the force on the contact face and that face’s area.

blocks.title: Use the contact area in the pressure formula
blocks.prompt: Use \(\text{pressure}=\frac{\text{force}}{\text{contact area}}\). A plate presses on a surface with a force of \(156\,\mathrm N\) over \(0.6\,\mathrm m^2\). Find the pressure in newtons per square metre.
blocks.hint: Give the contact area in square metres before using the formula.
blocks.solution:
The contact area is already in square metres.

Divide the force by the area in contact with the surface. \(\frac{156}{0.6}=260\).

The pressure is \(260\,\mathrm{N/m^2}\).

field.label: Pressure in newtons per square metre

blocks.html: Using all the faces of a block in place of the contact area makes the denominator too large.

blocks.title: Recover contact area from pressure
blocks.prompt: Use \(\text{pressure}=\frac{\text{force}}{\text{contact area}}\). A load exerts \(396\,\mathrm N\) and produces pressure \(180\,\mathrm{N/m^2}\). Find the area in contact with the floor in square metres.
blocks.hint: Rearrange the formula so area is alone before substituting.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the given equation by contact area. Then divide by pressure.

Contact area is force divided by pressure. \(\frac{396}{180}=2.2\).

The area is \(2.2\,\mathrm m^2\).

blocks.html: If the question asks for area, rearrange the given formula before putting in the numbers.

sections.title: How do I compare population and area?
sections.label: People per unit area
sections.intro: Population density describes the average number of people per unit of area. It does not say everybody is evenly spread.

blocks.html: Use \(\text{population density}=\frac{\text{population}}{\text{area}}\). A result measured per square kilometre uses the population of the same area that appears in the denominator.

blocks.title: Find population density
blocks.prompt: Use \(\text{population density}=\frac{\text{population}}{\text{area}}\). A district has area \(42\,\mathrm{km}^2\) and population \(3570\). Find the population density.
blocks.hint: Divide the number of people by the area of the district.
blocks.solution:
Both quantities refer to the whole district.

Divide the population by the area. \(\frac{3570}{42}=85\).

The population density is \(85\) people per square kilometre.

blocks.html: A region with more people can have lower population density when the area is much larger.

blocks.title: Use area and people per square kilometre
blocks.prompt: Use \(\text{population density}=\frac{\text{population}}{\text{area}}\). An island covers \(20\,\mathrm{km}^2\) and has a population density of \(111\) people per square kilometre. Find the population.
blocks.hint: Here you know the rate and the area. Multiply them to recover the total.
blocks.solution:
The density supplies the number of people for one square kilometre on average.

Multiply density by the number of square kilometres. \(111\times 20=2220\).

The population is \(2220\) people.

blocks.html: Show the formula supplied in the question and write the unit of the result.

examples.title: Find mass per cubic centimetre
examples.question: Use \(\text{density}=\frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}\). A sample has mass \(48\,\mathrm g\) and volume \(20\,\mathrm{cm}^3\). Find its density in grams per cubic centimetre.
solution: Substitute the mass as the numerator and the volume as the denominator.
The density is \(2.4\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}\).

examples.title: Recover mass from density and volume
examples.question: Use \(\text{density}=\frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}\). A casting has volume \(35\,\mathrm{cm}^3\) and density \(1.3\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}\). Find its mass.
solution: Multiply both sides of the given formula by volume to get mass.
Multiply grams per cubic centimetre by the volume. \(1.3\times 35=45.5\).
The mass is \(45.5\,\mathrm g\).

examples.title: Use the contact area in the pressure formula
examples.question: Use \(\text{pressure}=\frac{\text{force}}{\text{contact area}}\). A plate presses on a surface with a force of \(132\,\mathrm N\) over \(5500\,\mathrm{cm}^2\). Find the pressure in newtons per square metre.
solution: Since one square metre is 10 000 square centimetres, the contact area is \(0.55\,\mathrm m^2\).
Divide the force by the area in contact with the surface. \(\frac{132}{0.55}=240\).
The pressure is \(240\,\mathrm{N/m^2}\).

examples.title: Recover contact area from pressure
examples.question: Use \(\text{pressure}=\frac{\text{force}}{\text{contact area}}\). A load exerts \(336\,\mathrm N\) and produces pressure \(160\,\mathrm{N/m^2}\). Find the area in contact with the floor in square metres.
solution: Multiply the given equation by contact area. Then divide by pressure.
Contact area is force divided by pressure. \(\frac{336}{160}=2.1\).
The area is \(2.1\,\mathrm m^2\).

examples.title: Find population density
examples.question: Use \(\text{population density}=\frac{\text{population}}{\text{area}}\). A district has area \(38\,\mathrm{km}^2\) and population \(2888\). Find the population density.
solution: Both quantities refer to the whole district.
Divide the population by the area. \(\frac{2888}{38}=76\).
The population density is \(76\) people per square kilometre.

examples.title: Use area and people per square kilometre
examples.question: Use \(\text{population density}=\frac{\text{population}}{\text{area}}\). An island covers \(18\,\mathrm{km}^2\) and has a population density of \(107\) people per square kilometre. Find the population.
solution: The density supplies the number of people for one square kilometre on average.
Multiply density by the number of square kilometres. \(107\times 18=1926\).
The population is \(1926\) people.

extraPractice.title: Find mass per cubic centimetre
extraPractice.prompt: Use \(\text{density}=\frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}\). A sample has mass \(78\,\mathrm g\) and volume \(30\,\mathrm{cm}^3\). Find its density in grams per cubic centimetre.
extraPractice.hint: Density is the mass of one cubic centimetre under this model.
extraPractice.solution:
Substitute the mass as the numerator and the volume as the denominator.

\(\frac{78}{30}=2.6\).

The density is \(2.6\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}\).

field.label: Density in grams per cubic centimetre

extraPractice.title: Recover mass from density and volume
extraPractice.prompt: Use \(\text{density}=\frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}\). A casting has volume \(45\,\mathrm{cm}^3\) and density \(1.5\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}\). Find its mass.
extraPractice.hint: Multiply the mass of one cubic centimetre by the number of cubic centimetres.
extraPractice.solution:
Multiply both sides of the given formula by volume to get mass.

Multiply grams per cubic centimetre by the volume. \(1.5\times 45=67.5\).

The mass is \(67.5\,\mathrm g\).

extraPractice.title: Use the contact area in the pressure formula
extraPractice.prompt: Use \(\text{pressure}=\frac{\text{force}}{\text{contact area}}\). A plate presses on a surface with a force of \(182\,\mathrm N\) over \(6500\,\mathrm{cm}^2\). Find the pressure in newtons per square metre.
extraPractice.hint: Give the contact area in square metres before using the formula.
extraPractice.solution:
Since one square metre is 10 000 square centimetres, the contact area is \(0.65\,\mathrm m^2\).

Divide the force by the area in contact with the surface. \(\frac{182}{0.65}=280\).

The pressure is \(280\,\mathrm{N/m^2}\).

field.label: Pressure in newtons per square metre

extraPractice.title: Recover contact area from pressure
extraPractice.prompt: Use \(\text{pressure}=\frac{\text{force}}{\text{contact area}}\). A load exerts \(460\,\mathrm N\) and produces pressure \(200\,\mathrm{N/m^2}\). Find the area in contact with the floor in square metres.
extraPractice.hint: Rearrange the formula so area is alone before substituting.
extraPractice.solution:
Multiply the given equation by contact area. Then divide by pressure.

Contact area is force divided by pressure. \(\frac{460}{200}=2.3\).

The area is \(2.3\,\mathrm m^2\).

extraPractice.title: Find population density
extraPractice.prompt: Use \(\text{population density}=\frac{\text{population}}{\text{area}}\). A district has area \(46\,\mathrm{km}^2\) and population \(4324\). Find the population density.
extraPractice.hint: Divide the number of people by the area of the district.
extraPractice.solution:
Both quantities refer to the whole district.

Divide the population by the area. \(\frac{4324}{46}=94\).

The population density is \(94\) people per square kilometre.

extraPractice.title: Use area and people per square kilometre
extraPractice.prompt: Use \(\text{population density}=\frac{\text{population}}{\text{area}}\). An island covers \(22\,\mathrm{km}^2\) and has a population density of \(115\) people per square kilometre. Find the population.
extraPractice.hint: Here you know the rate and the area. Multiply them to recover the total.
extraPractice.solution:
The density supplies the number of people for one square kilometre on average.

Multiply density by the number of square kilometres. \(115\times 22=2530\).

The population is \(2530\) people.

glossary.definition: Mass per unit volume.
Force per unit area.
The part of a surface where the force acts.
People per unit of area.
A measure using more than one kind of quantity.

revision.body:
Mass and volume

Use the supplied formula \(\text{density}=\frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}\). With grams and cubic centimetres, report grams per cubic centimetre.

Force on a contact area

Use \(\text{pressure}=\frac{\text{force}}{\text{contact area}}\). With force in newtons and area in square metres, the unit is newtons per square metre. One square metre contains 10 000 square centimetres.

People per unit area

Use \(\text{population density}=\frac{\text{population}}{\text{area}}\). A result measured per square kilometre uses the population of the same area that appears in the denominator.

Example

\(\text{density}=\frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}\). A mass of 138 g in a volume of 60 cubic centimetres has density \(2.3\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}\).

Check yourself

  • Find the pressure from 90 N on 0.30 square metres.
  • Find the population of 26 square kilometres at 110 people per square kilometre.

Answers \(300\,\mathrm{N/m^2}\) and 2860 people.
revision.checks:
• If a question asks for mass, use the known density and volume to recover it. The value of density is not the total mass.
  • Using all the faces of a block in place of the contact area makes the denominator too large.
  • A region with more people can have lower population density when the area is much larger.
revision.examTip: Show the formula supplied in the question and write the unit of the result.

igcse-0580-rates-speed-units.description: Connect speed, distance and time, and convert between kilometres per hour and metres per second.

sections.title: Which relationship links speed, distance and time?
sections.label: Link the quantities
sections.intro: Speed is the distance travelled for one unit of time. A speed in kilometres per hour tells you how far you would travel at that rate in one hour.

blocks.html: Use \(s=\frac dt\), \(d=st\) and \(t=\frac ds\), where \(s\) is speed, \(d\) is distance and \(t\) is elapsed time.

figure.alt: A full hour is marked as four equal groups of fifteen minutes, with three groups filled.
figure.caption: 45 minutes is \(\frac{45}{60}=\frac34\) of an hour.

blocks.title: Compute speed using hours
blocks.prompt: A delivery rider covers \(48\,\mathrm{km}\) in 60 minutes. Find the average speed in kilometres per hour.
blocks.hint: Use the distance travelled and convert the time to hours first.
blocks.solution:
Convert minutes to hours, since the answer is per hour. \(60\,\mathrm{min}\) is \(1\,\mathrm h\).

Average speed equals distance divided by time. \(\frac{48}{1}=48\).

The speed is \(48\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

blocks.html: Multiplying distance by time does not give distance for one unit of time.

blocks.title: Calculate distance from speed and time
blocks.prompt: A research boat travels at \(35\,\mathrm{km/h}\) for 30 minutes. Find the distance travelled.
blocks.hint: Multiply kilometres per hour by the time in hours.
blocks.solution:
Write 30 minutes as \(0.5\,\mathrm h\).

Distance is speed multiplied by time. \(35\times 0.5=17.5\).

The boat travels \(17.5\,\mathrm{km}\).

blocks.html: Write the formula that has the unknown quantity by itself before substituting.

sections.title: Which units must match?
sections.label: Distance units and time units
sections.intro: The time in the denominator must use the time unit of the required speed. If the answer is in kilometres per hour, use kilometres and hours.

blocks.html: Divide minutes by 60 for hours. Multiply hours by 60 for minutes. With metres per second and seconds, speed multiplied by time gives metres.

blocks.title: Calculate the time in minutes
blocks.prompt: A passenger boat covers \(36\,\mathrm{km}\) at an average speed of \(60\,\mathrm{km/h}\). Find the journey time in minutes.
blocks.hint: Divide distance by speed, then change the resulting time from hours to minutes.
blocks.solution:
Divide distance by speed to get time in hours. \(\frac{36}{60}=0.6\).

An hour contains 60 minutes. Multiply the time in hours by 60.

The journey takes 36 minutes.

blocks.html: Treat a clock reading or a number of minutes as elapsed time in the right units first. One hour 20 minutes is not 1.20 hours.

blocks.title: Match metres with seconds
blocks.prompt: A robot moves at \(6\,\mathrm{m/s}\) for 28 seconds. How far does it move in metres?
blocks.hint: The seconds cancel when you multiply metres per second by seconds.
blocks.solution:
The speed is measured per second, so the time is already in the right unit.

Multiply the speed in metres per second by seconds. \(6\times 28=168\).

The distance is \(168\,\mathrm m\).

blocks.html: Include the final unit even when the question shows a unit beside the answer line.

sections.title: How do I convert both parts of a speed unit?
sections.label: Change each part separately
sections.intro: Convert the distance to the new distance unit. Then scale the time interval to one unit of the new time measure.

blocks.html: To change km/h to m/s, multiply the distance by 1000 and divide by 3600. For m/s to km/h, use the reverse steps.

blocks.title: Convert kilometres per hour to metres per second
blocks.prompt: A training vehicle travels at \(36\,\mathrm{km/h}\). Give the same speed in metres per second.
blocks.hint: Use 1000 metres for each kilometre and 3600 seconds for the hour.
blocks.solution:
Convert kilometres to metres. The vehicle covers \(36000\,\mathrm m\) in one hour.

One hour has 3600 seconds. Per second, the distance is \(\frac{36000}{3600}=10\) metres.

The speed is \(10\,\mathrm{m/s}\).

blocks.html: A conversion of both units has two factors. Changing kilometres to metres alone gives metres per hour.

blocks.title: Convert metres per second to kilometres per hour
blocks.prompt: A sailing trial measures a speed of \(11\,\mathrm{m/s}\). Find the speed in kilometres per hour.
blocks.hint: Work out metres in one hour first, then convert them to kilometres.
blocks.solution:
In 3600 seconds, the vehicle would travel \(39600\,\mathrm m\) at this speed.

Divide the metres by 1000 to convert to kilometres.

The speed is \(39.6\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

blocks.html: Derive the factor from one kilometre and one hour if you forget the shortcut. It is safer than guessing which way 3.6 goes.

examples.title: Compute speed using hours
examples.question: A delivery rider covers \(33\,\mathrm{km}\) in 45 minutes. Find the average speed in kilometres per hour.
solution: Convert minutes to hours, since the answer is per hour. \(45\,\mathrm{min}\) is \(0.75\,\mathrm h\).
Average speed equals distance divided by time. \(\frac{33}{0.75}=44\).
The speed is \(44\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

examples.title: Calculate distance from speed and time
examples.question: A research boat travels at \(30\,\mathrm{km/h}\) for 24 minutes. Find the distance travelled.
solution: Write 24 minutes as \(0.4\,\mathrm h\).
Distance is speed multiplied by time. \(30\times 0.4=12\).
The boat travels \(12\,\mathrm{km}\).

examples.title: Calculate the time in minutes
examples.question: A passenger boat covers \(24\,\mathrm{km}\) at an average speed of \(45\,\mathrm{km/h}\). Find the journey time in minutes.
solution: Divide distance by speed to get time in hours. \(\frac{24}{45}=\frac{8}{15}\).
An hour contains 60 minutes. Multiply the time in hours by 60.
The journey takes 32 minutes.

examples.title: Match metres with seconds
examples.question: A robot moves at \(5.5\,\mathrm{m/s}\) for 24 seconds. How far does it move in metres?
solution: The speed is measured per second, so the time is already in the right unit.
Multiply the speed in metres per second by seconds. \(5.5\times 24=132\).
The distance is \(132\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Convert kilometres per hour to metres per second
examples.question: A training vehicle travels at \(25.2\,\mathrm{km/h}\). Give the same speed in metres per second.
solution: Convert kilometres to metres. The vehicle covers \(25200\,\mathrm m\) in one hour.
One hour has 3600 seconds. Per second, the distance is \(\frac{25200}{3600}=7\) metres.
The speed is \(7\,\mathrm{m/s}\).

examples.title: Convert metres per second to kilometres per hour
examples.question: A sailing trial measures a speed of \(9\,\mathrm{m/s}\). Find the speed in kilometres per hour.
solution: In 3600 seconds, the vehicle would travel \(32400\,\mathrm m\) at this speed.
Divide the metres by 1000 to convert to kilometres.
The speed is \(32.4\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

extraPractice.title: Compute speed using hours
extraPractice.prompt: A delivery rider covers \(65\,\mathrm{km}\) in 75 minutes. Find the average speed in kilometres per hour.
extraPractice.hint: Use the distance travelled and convert the time to hours first.
extraPractice.solution:
Convert minutes to hours, since the answer is per hour. \(75\,\mathrm{min}\) is \(1.25\,\mathrm h\).

Average speed equals distance divided by time. \(\frac{65}{1.25}=52\).

The speed is \(52\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

extraPractice.title: Calculate distance from speed and time
extraPractice.prompt: A research boat travels at \(40\,\mathrm{km/h}\) for 36 minutes. Find the distance travelled.
extraPractice.hint: Multiply kilometres per hour by the time in hours.
extraPractice.solution:
Write 36 minutes as \(0.6\,\mathrm h\).

Distance is speed multiplied by time. \(40\times 0.6=24\).

The boat travels \(24\,\mathrm{km}\).

extraPractice.title: Calculate the time in minutes
extraPractice.prompt: A passenger boat covers \(50\,\mathrm{km}\) at an average speed of \(75\,\mathrm{km/h}\). Find the journey time in minutes.
extraPractice.hint: Divide distance by speed, then change the resulting time from hours to minutes.
extraPractice.solution:
Divide distance by speed to get time in hours. \(\frac{50}{75}=\frac{2}{3}\).

An hour contains 60 minutes. Multiply the time in hours by 60.

The journey takes 40 minutes.

extraPractice.title: Match metres with seconds
extraPractice.prompt: A robot moves at \(6.5\,\mathrm{m/s}\) for 32 seconds. How far does it move in metres?
extraPractice.hint: The seconds cancel when you multiply metres per second by seconds.
extraPractice.solution:
The speed is measured per second, so the time is already in the right unit.

Multiply the speed in metres per second by seconds. \(6.5\times 32=208\).

The distance is \(208\,\mathrm m\).

extraPractice.title: Convert kilometres per hour to metres per second
extraPractice.prompt: A training vehicle travels at \(46.8\,\mathrm{km/h}\). Give the same speed in metres per second.
extraPractice.hint: Use 1000 metres for each kilometre and 3600 seconds for the hour.
extraPractice.solution:
Convert kilometres to metres. The vehicle covers \(46800\,\mathrm m\) in one hour.

One hour has 3600 seconds. Per second, the distance is \(\frac{46800}{3600}=13\) metres.

The speed is \(13\,\mathrm{m/s}\).

extraPractice.title: Convert metres per second to kilometres per hour
extraPractice.prompt: A sailing trial measures a speed of \(13\,\mathrm{m/s}\). Find the speed in kilometres per hour.
extraPractice.hint: Work out metres in one hour first, then convert them to kilometres.
extraPractice.solution:
In 3600 seconds, the vehicle would travel \(46800\,\mathrm m\) at this speed.

Divide the metres by 1000 to convert to kilometres.

The speed is \(46.8\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

glossary.definition: The length of the path travelled.
The length of time between the start and end.
Distance travelled divided by elapsed time.
A distance unit followed by a time unit, such as kilometres per hour.
A multiplier that rewrites a quantity in other units.

revision.body:
Link the quantities

Use \(s=\frac dt\), \(d=st\) and \(t=\frac ds\), where \(s\) is speed, \(d\) is distance and \(t\) is elapsed time.

Distance units and time units

Divide minutes by 60 for hours. Multiply hours by 60 for minutes. With metres per second and seconds, speed multiplied by time gives metres.

Change each part separately

To change km/h to m/s, multiply the distance by 1000 and divide by 3600. For m/s to km/h, use the reverse steps.

Example

A journey covers 36 km in 45 minutes. Its average speed is \(\frac{36}{0.75}=48\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

Check yourself

  • Find the distance travelled at 45 km/h in 24 minutes.
  • Change 75.6 km/h to m/s.

Answers \(18\,\mathrm{km}\) and \(21\,\mathrm{m/s}\).
revision.checks:
• Multiplying distance by time does not give distance for one unit of time.
  • Treat a clock reading or a number of minutes as elapsed time in the right units first. One hour 20 minutes is not 1.20 hours.
  • A conversion of both units has two factors. Changing kilometres to metres alone gives metres per hour.
revision.examTip: Derive the factor from one kilometre and one hour if you forget the shortcut. It is safer than guessing which way 3.6 goes.

igcse-0580-rates-average-journeys.description: Use total distance and the right elapsed time, and recover a missing stage.

sections.title: Why do I need the distance and time totals?
sections.label: Calculate an overall average
sections.intro: An overall average speed gives the single constant speed that would cover the same total distance in the same total time.

blocks.html: Add the distances and add the journey times. Then divide total distance by total time. The mean of two speeds applies when the speeds last for equal times.

figure.alt: A ninety-minute timeline shows 18 kilometres, a 15-minute stop and 27 more kilometres.
figure.caption: Count 45 km and 90 minutes for the whole journey. The stop has zero distance.

blocks.title: Give the longer stage its proper weight
blocks.prompt: A coach travels at \(39\,\mathrm{km/h}\) for 45 minutes and then \(63\,\mathrm{km/h}\) for 90 minutes. Find its average speed over both stages.
blocks.hint: Do not average the two speeds directly. The stages last different amounts of time.
blocks.solution:
The distances are \(29.25\,\mathrm{km}\) and \(94.5\,\mathrm{km}\), found by multiplying each stage speed by its time in hours.

The total distance is \(123.75\,\mathrm{km}\), and total time is \(2.25\,\mathrm h\).

Dividing these totals gives \(55\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

field.label: Overall speed in kilometres per hour

blocks.html: A stage that lasts longer contributes more to the overall average than a short stage.

blocks.title: Count a stop in the elapsed time
blocks.prompt: A shuttle travels \(21\,\mathrm{km}\) in 28 minutes, stops for 14 minutes, then travels \(35\,\mathrm{km}\) in 42 minutes. Find the average speed for the whole journey, including the stop.
blocks.hint: The stop adds no distance, but it adds to the journey time.
blocks.solution:
The shuttle travels \(56\,\mathrm{km}\) in total.

Include the stop. 28 plus 14 plus 42 minutes gives 84 minutes, or \(1.4\,\mathrm h\).

Divide total distance by elapsed time to obtain \(40\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

field.label: Average over the whole journey in kilometres per hour

retry.feedback: You used moving time only. The whole-journey average includes the stop.

blocks.html: If only the speeds and stage times are given, find each stage distance before trying to average.

sections.title: Do stops and returning to the start change the totals?
sections.label: Stopped time and return trips
sections.intro: Read the time interval described by the question. A stop adds time and no distance. A return trip adds distance as well as time.

blocks.html: For a whole-journey average, include any stop between start and finish. If asked for average speed while moving, use the moving time only.

blocks.title: Use moving time when the question asks for it
blocks.prompt: A cycling crew covers \(48.6\,\mathrm{km}\) in two riding spells of 36 and 72 minutes. There is a 7-minute repair stop between them. Calculate their average speed while moving.
blocks.hint: Read whether the requested average includes or excludes stationary time.
blocks.solution:
For moving time, count the two riding spells but not the repair stop.

The riding time is 108 minutes, or \(1.8\,\mathrm h\).

Divide the distance ridden by the riding time to obtain \(27\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

field.label: Average moving speed in kilometres per hour

retry.feedback: The question asks for moving speed, so leave the repair stop out of the denominator.

blocks.html: Ending where you started does not mean that your distance travelled is zero.

blocks.title: Count both directions of a return trip
blocks.prompt: A cyclist rides \(8.55\,\mathrm{km}\) to a checkpoint in 36 minutes and returns along the same route in 18 minutes. Find the average speed for the complete trip with no stop.
blocks.hint: Use total distance travelled. Returning to the start does not give zero distance.
blocks.solution:
Count both legs. The distance travelled is \(17.1\,\mathrm{km}\), although the finish is back at the start.

The elapsed time is 54 minutes, or \(0.9\,\mathrm h\).

The average speed is \(19\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

field.label: Average return-trip speed in kilometres per hour

blocks.html: List each stage including any stop. Check that the sum of elapsed times matches the stated interval.

sections.title: What can I recover from an overall average?
sections.label: Work back from a total
sections.intro: If you know the overall average and total time, multiply to recover total distance. Then subtract the known part.

blocks.html: Use the same time and distance units before subtracting any stage. With remaining distance and remaining time, use the ordinary speed calculation for the missing stage.

blocks.title: Find the speed on a missing stage
blocks.prompt: A service van takes \(3\,\mathrm h\) for a two-stage trip with average speed \(50\,\mathrm{km/h}\). It travels at \(42\,\mathrm{km/h}\) for the first \(1\,\mathrm h\). Find the average speed on the second stage. There is no stop.
blocks.hint: Use the overall average to find total distance, then subtract the known stage.
blocks.solution:
The full distance is \(150\,\mathrm{km}\). The first stage covers \(42\,\mathrm{km}\).

The second stage covers \(108\,\mathrm{km}\) in \(2\,\mathrm h\).

Its average speed is \(54\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

field.label: Second-stage speed in kilometres per hour

blocks.html: The overall average is not the speed on the missing stage. Rebuild the totals first.

blocks.title: Combine stages with different distance units
blocks.prompt: A field test uses \(21.12\,\mathrm{km}\) of track in 30 minutes, then \(31680\,\mathrm m\) in 42 minutes. Give the overall average speed in kilometres per hour.
blocks.hint: Add distances after converting them to the same unit, then divide by total hours.
blocks.solution:
Convert the second distance to \(31.68\,\mathrm{km}\) before adding.

The total distance is \(52.8\,\mathrm{km}\). The total time is \(1.2\,\mathrm h\).

Divide distance by time to find \(44\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

field.label: Average speed in kilometres per hour

blocks.html: Check your missing distance or time by putting it back into the whole journey.

examples.title: Give the longer stage its proper weight
examples.question: A coach travels at \(36\,\mathrm{km/h}\) for 30 minutes and then \(60\,\mathrm{km/h}\) for 60 minutes. Find its average speed over both stages.
solution: The distances are \(18\,\mathrm{km}\) and \(60\,\mathrm{km}\), found by multiplying each stage speed by its time in hours.
The total distance is \(78\,\mathrm{km}\), and total time is \(1.5\,\mathrm h\).
Dividing these totals gives \(52\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

examples.title: Count a stop in the elapsed time
examples.question: A shuttle travels \(16.2\,\mathrm{km}\) in 24 minutes, stops for 12 minutes, then travels \(27\,\mathrm{km}\) in 36 minutes. Find the average speed for the whole journey, including the stop.
solution: The shuttle travels \(43.2\,\mathrm{km}\) in total.
Include the stop. 24 plus 12 plus 36 minutes gives 72 minutes, or \(1.2\,\mathrm h\).
Divide total distance by elapsed time to obtain \(36\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

examples.title: Use moving time when the question asks for it
examples.question: A cycling crew covers \(36\,\mathrm{km}\) in two riding spells of 30 and 60 minutes. There is a 5-minute repair stop between them. Calculate their average speed while moving.
solution: For moving time, count the two riding spells but not the repair stop.
The riding time is 90 minutes, or \(1.5\,\mathrm h\).
Divide the distance ridden by the riding time to obtain \(24\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

examples.title: Count both directions of a return trip
examples.question: A cyclist rides \(5.4\,\mathrm{km}\) to a checkpoint in 24 minutes and returns along the same route in 12 minutes. Find the average speed for the complete trip with no stop.
solution: Count both legs. The distance travelled is \(10.8\,\mathrm{km}\), although the finish is back at the start.
The elapsed time is 36 minutes, or \(0.6\,\mathrm h\).
The average speed is \(18\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

examples.title: Find the speed on a missing stage
examples.question: A service van takes \(2.5\,\mathrm h\) for a two-stage trip with average speed \(48\,\mathrm{km/h}\). It travels at \(40\,\mathrm{km/h}\) for the first \(0.5\,\mathrm h\). Find the average speed on the second stage. There is no stop.
solution: The full distance is \(120\,\mathrm{km}\). The first stage covers \(20\,\mathrm{km}\).
The second stage covers \(100\,\mathrm{km}\) in \(2\,\mathrm h\).
Its average speed is \(50\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

examples.title: Combine stages with different distance units
examples.question: A field test uses \(16\,\mathrm{km}\) of track in 24 minutes, then \(24000\,\mathrm m\) in 36 minutes. Give the overall average speed in kilometres per hour.
solution: Convert the second distance to \(24\,\mathrm{km}\) before adding.
The total distance is \(40\,\mathrm{km}\). The total time is \(1\,\mathrm h\).
Divide distance by time to find \(40\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

extraPractice.title: Give the longer stage its proper weight
extraPractice.prompt: A coach travels at \(42\,\mathrm{km/h}\) for 60 minutes and then \(66\,\mathrm{km/h}\) for 120 minutes. Find its average speed over both stages.
extraPractice.hint: Do not average the two speeds directly. The stages last different amounts of time.
extraPractice.solution:
The distances are \(42\,\mathrm{km}\) and \(132\,\mathrm{km}\), found by multiplying each stage speed by its time in hours.

The total distance is \(174\,\mathrm{km}\), and total time is \(3\,\mathrm h\).

Dividing these totals gives \(58\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

field.label: Overall speed in kilometres per hour

extraPractice.title: Count a stop in the elapsed time
extraPractice.prompt: A shuttle travels \(26.4\,\mathrm{km}\) in 32 minutes, stops for 16 minutes, then travels \(44\,\mathrm{km}\) in 48 minutes. Find the average speed for the whole journey, including the stop.
extraPractice.hint: The stop adds no distance, but it adds to the journey time.
extraPractice.solution:
The shuttle travels \(70.4\,\mathrm{km}\) in total.

Include the stop. 32 plus 16 plus 48 minutes gives 96 minutes, or \(1.6\,\mathrm h\).

Divide total distance by elapsed time to obtain \(44\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

field.label: Average over the whole journey in kilometres per hour

retry.feedback: You used moving time only. The whole-journey average includes the stop.

extraPractice.title: Use moving time when the question asks for it
extraPractice.prompt: A cycling crew covers \(63\,\mathrm{km}\) in two riding spells of 42 and 84 minutes. There is a 9-minute repair stop between them. Calculate their average speed while moving.
extraPractice.hint: Read whether the requested average includes or excludes stationary time.
extraPractice.solution:
For moving time, count the two riding spells but not the repair stop.

The riding time is 126 minutes, or \(2.1\,\mathrm h\).

Divide the distance ridden by the riding time to obtain \(30\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

field.label: Average moving speed in kilometres per hour

retry.feedback: The question asks for moving speed, so leave the repair stop out of the denominator.

extraPractice.title: Count both directions of a return trip
extraPractice.prompt: A cyclist rides \(12\,\mathrm{km}\) to a checkpoint in 48 minutes and returns along the same route in 24 minutes. Find the average speed for the complete trip with no stop.
extraPractice.hint: Use total distance travelled. Returning to the start does not give zero distance.
extraPractice.solution:
Count both legs. The distance travelled is \(24\,\mathrm{km}\), although the finish is back at the start.

The elapsed time is 72 minutes, or \(1.2\,\mathrm h\).

The average speed is \(20\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

field.label: Average return-trip speed in kilometres per hour

extraPractice.title: Find the speed on a missing stage
extraPractice.prompt: A service van takes \(3.5\,\mathrm h\) for a two-stage trip with average speed \(52\,\mathrm{km/h}\). It travels at \(44\,\mathrm{km/h}\) for the first \(1.5\,\mathrm h\). Find the average speed on the second stage. There is no stop.
extraPractice.hint: Use the overall average to find total distance, then subtract the known stage.
extraPractice.solution:
The full distance is \(182\,\mathrm{km}\). The first stage covers \(66\,\mathrm{km}\).

The second stage covers \(116\,\mathrm{km}\) in \(2\,\mathrm h\).

Its average speed is \(58\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

field.label: Second-stage speed in kilometres per hour

extraPractice.title: Combine stages with different distance units
extraPractice.prompt: A field test uses \(26.88\,\mathrm{km}\) of track in 36 minutes, then \(40320\,\mathrm m\) in 48 minutes. Give the overall average speed in kilometres per hour.
extraPractice.hint: Add distances after converting them to the same unit, then divide by total hours.
extraPractice.solution:
Convert the second distance to \(40.32\,\mathrm{km}\) before adding.

The total distance is \(67.2\,\mathrm{km}\). The total time is \(1.4\,\mathrm h\).

Divide distance by time to find \(48\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

field.label: Average speed in kilometres per hour

glossary.definition: One part of a longer journey.
At rest. No distance is travelled during that time.
The total distance divided by the elapsed time of the specified interval.
The combined duration of the parts where distance is being travelled.
The part of a trip that returns towards or to its starting point.

revision.body:
Calculate an overall average

Add the distances and add the journey times. Then divide total distance by total time. The mean of two speeds applies when the speeds last for equal times.

Stopped time and return trips

For a whole-journey average, include any stop between start and finish. If asked for average speed while moving, use the moving time only.

Work back from a total

Use the same time and distance units before subtracting any stage. With remaining distance and remaining time, use the ordinary speed calculation for the missing stage.

Example

A journey of 18 km, a stop, then 27 km takes 90 minutes altogether. Its average is \(\frac{45}{1.5}=30\,\mathrm{km/h}\).

Check yourself

  • A learner cycles 8 km out and 8 km back in 48 minutes altogether. Find the overall speed.
  • For the diagram, find the average speed while moving.

Answers \(20\,\mathrm{km/h}\) and \(36\,\mathrm{km/h}\).
revision.checks:
• A stage that lasts longer contributes more to the overall average than a short stage.
  • Ending where you started does not mean that your distance travelled is zero.
  • The overall average is not the speed on the missing stage. Rebuild the totals first.
revision.examTip: Check your missing distance or time by putting it back into the whole journey.
